title: Crop Yield: What It Means, How to Measure It and How to Raise It
metaTitle: Crop Yield: Meaning, How to Compute and Raise It
metaDescription: Crop yield is how much you harvest per hectare. Learn how to measure it with a crop cut, adjust for moisture, compare with averages and raise it.
excerpt: Crop yield is the amount of harvest you get from a given area, usually written as tons or cavans per hectare. It is the simplest measure of how well a season went. For palay, the national average sits around 4 tons per hectare, while well managed irrigated farms often reach 5 to 6 tons or more. This guide shows how to measure your own crop yield and where the extra cavans usually hide.

heroImage.alt: Workers harvesting a field by hand, the moment crop yield is finally counted

blocks.text:
Most farmers know their harvest in sacks, but fewer know their yield per hectare. Yet that one number tells you whether a new variety, fertilizer plan or planting date actually worked.

This guide explains what crop yield means, how to measure it fairly, how to compare it, and what raises it. For forecasting a harvest before it comes in, see [crop yield forecasting](/blog/crop-yield-forecasting).

Yield is harvest divided by area. If a 2 hectare farm gives 10 tons of palay, its yield is 5 tons per hectare. Writing it per hectare lets you compare a small lot with a big one, and this season with the last.

For palay, many farmers count in cavans. A cavan of palay is usually taken as 50 kilograms, so 100 cavans per hectare equals 5 tons per hectare.
How to measure crop yield with a crop cut
You do not need to weigh the whole field to know your yield. A crop cut, done carefully, gives a good estimate a few days before harvest.

items.title: Mark sample areas
items.text: Pick three spots that look average, not the best or worst. Mark an area of 5 square meters in each, for example 2.5 by 2 meters.

items.title: Harvest and thresh
items.text: Cut all the plants inside each area, thresh them, and clean the grain.

items.title: Weigh and check moisture
items.text: Weigh the grain from each area and note its moisture. Fresh palay is often above 20 percent moisture.

items.title: Adjust to 14 percent moisture
items.text: Multiply the weight by (100 minus the moisture) and divide by 86. That gives the weight at 14 percent moisture, the usual standard for dry palay.

items.title: Scale to a hectare
items.text: Average the three areas and multiply by 2,000, because a hectare holds 2,000 areas of 5 square meters. The answer is kilograms per hectare.

blocks.text: For example, say an average 5 square meter area gives 3 kilograms of palay at 22 percent moisture. First, 3 times 78 divided by 86 is about 2.7 kilograms at 14 percent. Then 2.7 times 2,000 is about 5,400 kilograms, or 5.4 tons per hectare.
Why your yield differs from your neighbor's

items: **Variety:** some varieties simply carry more grain. See [the best rice variety for your area](/blog/best-rice-variety-for-my-area).
**Planting date:** heat or drought at flowering empties grains. See [when fertilization occurs](/blog/when-fertilization-occurs).
**Fertilizer:** the right amount at the right stage. See [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage).
**Water:** stress at tillering and flowering costs the most.
**Pests, diseases and weeds:** each takes a share, and together they take a lot.
**Harvest and drying losses:** late harvest and slow drying lose grain after it has grown. See [palay drying](/blog/palay-drying).

blocks.text:
Big jumps rarely come from one new product. They come from fixing the weakest link, then the next one. Start with the steps that cost little: good seed, a level field, timely weeding and fertilizer on the right days.

Our guides on [increasing rice yield per hectare](/blog/increase-rice-yield-per-hectare) and [increasing corn yield per hectare](/blog/increase-corn-yield-per-hectare) go through each step for those crops. For vegetables, see [vegetable farming](/blog/vegetable-farming).

blocks.title: Yield is not profit
blocks.text: A higher yield that costs more to grow may earn less. Track your cost per kilogram as well as your yield per hectare. Our guide on [farm profitability](/blog/farm-profitability) explains how.
Can anee.io raise your crop yield?

Yes. Most lost cavans come from tasks done late or forgotten, and anee.io keeps every task on its day. The [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar) dates each fertilizer, spray and irrigation from each lot's planting day. [Harvest records](/features/harvest-records) store the yield of every lot, and the reports set your yield beside your costs. Compare Reports then shows season against season, so you see what worked. Read [can anee.io increase my yield](/blog/can-anee-io-increase-my-yield) for how it all fits.

blocks.text: Log each lot's harvest, see your yield and cost per hectare, and compare season after season.

items.a: The amount harvested from a given area, usually in tons or cavans per hectare.

items.q: How do you compute yield per hectare?
items.a: Harvest three 5 square meter sample areas, adjust the grain to 14 percent moisture, average them and multiply by 2,000 to get kilograms per hectare.

items.q: What is the average palay yield per hectare in the Philippines?
items.a: Around 4 tons per hectare nationally. Well managed irrigated farms often reach 5 to 6 tons or more.

items.q: How many kilograms is one cavan of palay?
items.a: Usually 50 kilograms, so 100 cavans per hectare equals 5 tons per hectare.
Usually a mix of late planting, water stress at flowering, fertilizer at the wrong time, pests and weeds, and losses at harvest and drying.
